newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-CARRARO HOPES TO BRING PEACE TO ITALY SOCCER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CARRARO HOPES TO BRING PEACE TO ITALY SOCCER.

text.p: Franco Carraro, a former minister and mayor of Rome, said at the weekend he hoped to bring peace to the troubled world of Italian soccer after being elected chairman of the domestic league.

Carraro, one of the most senior figures in Italian sport, was voted to the post on Friday, ending two months of bitter squabbling between big and small teams over who should head the league, which is made up of the 38 serie A and B clubs.

Italy's smaller clubs finally accepted Carraro, who was backed by leading serie A teams, after he promised to set up two commissions -- one to look at how television revenues are distributed and another to examine reforms of the league set-up.
"I hope that Italian soccer can now find the right balance and the solutions to its problems," Carraro told reporters.
But the chairman of mighty AC Milan, Adriano Galliani, warned that the new league chief faced a difficult task.
"The differences between the various clubs are very wide. Carraro will have to mediate," he told reporters.
Carraro has already served as the chairman of the Italian league between 1976 and 1978. He left the job to take over as head of the Italian Olympic Committee, a position he held for almost 10 years.

In 1987 he was appointed minister of tourism and two years later became mayor of Rome. The 56-year old Carraro has also been chairman of AC Milan soccer club and is a life member of the International Olympic Committee.
The league chairmanship was left vacant last December after the previous holder, Luciano Nizzola, was elected president of Italy's soccer federation.

Less wealthy clubs, looking for more spoils from lucrative television deals, put forward two candidates to stand against Carraro -- the outgoing soccer federation president, Antonio Matarrese, and the head of Bologna soccer club Giuseppe Gazzoni.
After weeks of tense internal wrangling, Matarrese agreed to drop his own candidacy when he was promised a role as a roving international ambassador for Italian soccer.
"Everyone has won. It was important for Italian soccer to find peace with itself and to continue this battle would have done no-one any good," Matarrese said.
Gazzoni also stood down and Carraro won the final vote by 36 to 0, with two abstentions.
"There are numerous problems," he told reporters.
"We want a modern, efficient, well-organised league, but we have won the guarantees we sought," he added after the final ballot.
